docs.title: Python Fragments
docs.text:
Modern HTML template rendering in Python - no build step, no template files, and native HTML awareness out of the box.

Plain PythonFastAPIFlaskDjango 
# main.py
from fragments import loader

from views import render_index

# views.py
from my_components import Layout, PostCard

POSTS = [...]  # your data here

def render_index() -> str:
    published = [p for p in POSTS if p.published]
    return <>
        <Layout title="My Blog">
            <h1>Latest Posts</h1>
            <PostCard for={{ post in published }} post={{ post }} />
        </Layout>
    </>

# main.py
from fragments import loader

from fastapi import FastAPI
from .index import router

app = FastAPI()
app.include_router(router)

# index.py
from fastapi import APIRouter
from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse

router = APIRouter()

POSTS = [...]  # your data here

@router.get("/", response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def index() -> str:
    published = [p for p in POSTS if p.published]
    return <>
        <Layout title="My Blog">
            <h1>Latest Posts</h1>
            <PostCard for={{ post in published }} post={{ post }} />
        </Layout>
    </>

# app.py
from fragments import loader

from flask import Flask
from views import index_bp

app = Flask(__name__)
app.register_blueprint(index_bp)

# views.py
from flask import Blueprint

index_bp = Blueprint("index", __name__)

POSTS = [...]  # your data here

@index_bp.route("/")
def index() -> str:
    published = [p for p in POSTS if p.published]
    return <>
        <Layout title="My Blog">
            <h1>Latest Posts</h1>
            <PostCard for={{ post in published }} post={{ post }} />
        </Layout>
    </>

# urls.py
from fragments import loader

from django.urls import path
from views import index

urlpatterns = [path("", index)]

# views.py
from django.http import HttpRequest, HttpResponse

POSTS = [...]  # your data here

def index(request: HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse:
    published = [p for p in POSTS if p.published]
    return HttpResponse(<>
        <Layout title="My Blog">
            <h1>Latest Posts</h1>
            <PostCard for={{ post in published }} post={{ post }} />
        </Layout>
    </>)

docs.title: No build step
docs.text: Transpiled automatically at import time. No CLI, no watchers, no separate compile phase.

docs.title: Full IDE Support
docs.text: Type checking, hover, completions, go-to-definition, rename, and semantic highlighting via a built-in language server and VS Code extension.

docs.title: Production Tested
docs.text: Used in production and developed in-house by TheRunningAlgorithm, exposed to thousands of live users prior to open source release

docs.title: Long Term Support
docs.text: Actively maintained by TheRunningAlgorithm, who use it in production.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
pip install python-fragments

Register the loader at your app's entry point, before importing any modules that use fragments:

from fragments import loader
from my_components import my_component

Any .py file containing <> is transpiled automatically — nothing else to configure.

Full installation guide

docs.title: 2. Use With Your IDE
docs.text:
Install the language server for inline type errors, completions, and hover docs:

pip install python-fragments[lsp]

A VS Code extension is available on the Marketplace with structural syntax highlighting, semantic tokens, diagnostics, go-to-definition, rename, and more.

Full IDE setup guide

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: Python Fragments is pre-v1 and under active development at The Running Algorithm. This page outlines what we're working toward.

docs.title: Before v1
docs.text: The focus before v1 is not features: it's foundations. We're using Python Fragments in production internally and working to settle on a concrete developer experience and stable API before making any commitments. Until v1, the syntax and API may change between releases.

docs.title: After v1
docs.text:
Once the foundations are solid, we plan to invest heavily in tooling:

  • Black and Ruff formatter support: Black formatting of the Python around fragments is available now (see the Black integration). Formatting inside fragments and Ruff support are still to come.
  • isort and Ruff import sorting: imports in fragment files should sort correctly alongside regular Python
  • Linter compatibility: fragment syntax should not produce false positives in common linters
  • Better error messages: transpiler errors should point to the original fragment source, not the transpiled output

docs.title: Staying up to date
docs.text: Watch the GitHub repository for updates.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
Two benchmarks are included: one measuring the cost of transpilation (a one-time import-time cost), and one measuring the cost of calling a transpiled function at runtime.

All results were measured on a single machine and will vary by hardware. Run the benchmarks yourself to get numbers for your environment.

docs.title: Transpilation
docs.text:
Measures how long transpile() takes to convert a fragments source file into Python. This cost is paid once per file at import time, not on every request.

Source: benchmarks/transpilation/sample.py: a realistic file with two components, a for loop, interpolations, and an HTML comment.

python benchmarks/transpilation/benchmark.py

Transpiler benchmark (5000 iterations × 5 repeats)
  Fragments: 119.2 µs
  Jinja2:    926.8 µs

Fragments transpiles a file like this in 119.2 µs — about 8× faster than Jinja2 compiles an equivalent template. At around 8,400 transpilations per second, a file can be transpiled 1,400 times per character typed at a fast typing speed — this will never be the limiting factor in LSP or IDE performance.

docs.title: Calls
docs.text:
Measures how long a transpiled fragment function takes to execute at runtime compared to an equivalent plain string interpolation. This is the cost paid on every request.

Source: benchmarks/calls/sample.py: three functions that each render a list of three posts with a heading, byline, and summary: one using fragments, one using Jinja2, and one using str.format().

python benchmarks/calls/benchmark.py

Call benchmark (10000 iterations × 5 repeats)
  Fragments:            3.0 µs
  Jinja2:               5.0 µs
  String interpolation: 0.6 µs

Fragments adds a small overhead over raw string interpolation and is significantly faster than Jinja2. For a typical web request this cost is negligible: at 3.0 µs per render, a single millisecond of request budget can fit ~333 fragment renders.

docs.title: FastAPI Example
docs.text: A small blog application showing how Fragments fits into a real FastAPI project. It covers layout components, component composition, conditional rendering, and list rendering across two routes.

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
app/
├── main.py        # FastAPI app and loader registration
├── models.py      # Data model
├── components.py  # Reusable components
└── routes.py      # Route handlers

docs.title: models.py
docs.text:
A plain dataclass to represent a blog post:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Post:
    slug: str
    title: str
    summary: str
    body: str
    author: str
    published: bool = True

docs.title: components.py
docs.text:
Two components: a full-page layout wrapper, and a post card used in the listing.

from fragments.types import Children
from models import Post

def Layout(children: Children, title: str = "My Blog") -> str:
    return <>
        <html lang="en">
            <head>
                <meta charset="utf-8" />
                <title>{{ title }}</title>
                <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1" />
                <link rel="stylesheet" href="/static/styles.css" />
            </head>
            <body>
                <header>
                    <a href="/" classes="site-title">My Blog</a>
                </header>
                <main>
                    <Children... />
                </main>
            </body>
        </html>
    </>


def PostCard(post: Post) -> str:
    return <>
        <article classes="post-card">
            <h2>
                <a href={{ f"/posts/{post.slug}" }}>{{ post.title }}</a>
            </h2>
            <p classes="summary">{{ post.summary }}</p>
            <p classes="byline">By {{ post.author }}</p>
        </article>
    </>

Layout receives children from whatever is nested inside <Layout>...</Layout> and title as a keyword argument. PostCard is always used self-closing, so it declares only post — no children parameter needed.

docs.title: routes.py
docs.text:
Two routes: a post listing and a detail view.

from fastapi import APIRouter, HTTPException
from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse
from models import Post
from components import Layout, PostCard

router = APIRouter()

POSTS = [
    Post(
        slug="getting-started",
        title="Getting Started with Fragments",
        summary="How to add Python Fragments to an existing FastAPI app.",
        body="<p>Python Fragments lets you write HTML directly in .py files...</p>",
        author="Alice",
    ),
    Post(
        slug="component-patterns",
        title="Component Patterns",
        summary="Layout wrappers, cards, and other patterns that keep views clean.",
        body="<p>The key insight is that a component is just a function...</p>",
        author="Bob",
    ),
    Post(
        slug="upcoming-features",
        title="Upcoming Features",
        summary="What's coming next.",
        body="",
        author="Alice",
        published=False,
    ),
]

_by_slug: dict[str, Post] = {p.slug: p for p in POSTS}


@router.get("/", response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def index() -> str:
    published = [p for p in POSTS if p.published]
    return <>
        <Layout title="My Blog">
            <h1>Latest Posts</h1>
            <PostCard for={{ post in published }} post={{ post }} />
        </Layout>
    </>


@router.get("/posts/{slug}", response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def post_detail(slug: str) -> str:
    post = _by_slug.get(slug)
    if post is None or not post.published:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404)
    return <>
        <Layout title={{ post.title }}>
            <article>
                <h1>{{ post.title }}</h1>
                <p classes="byline"><em>By {{ post.author }}</em></p>
                {{ post.body }}
            </article>
            <a href="/" classes="back-link">← All posts</a>
        </Layout>
    </>

The for attribute on <PostCard> renders one card per post, passing each post object through as an attribute. Unpublished posts are filtered in Python before the fragment runs — keeping the markup free of business logic.

docs.title: main.py
docs.text:
Register the loader before any fragment-containing modules are imported:

from fragments import loader  # isort: skip

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse
from routes import router

app = FastAPI()
app.include_router(router)

The # isort: skip comment prevents import sorters from moving the loader import below routes, which would cause fragment syntax to be parsed before the transpiler is active.

docs.title: Getting Started Checklist
docs.text:
• Discover Python Fragments
  • Install the package with pip
  • Install the VS Code extension or LSP
  • Import with from fragments import loader
  • Start writing <>fragments</> in your project
  • Optionally, set up code formatting with Black

That's it, ready for production.

docs.title: Install the package
docs.text: pip install python-fragments

docs.title: Optional Extras
docs.text:
To install the language server:

pip install python-fragments[lsp]

To install the Black integration for code formatting:

pip install python-fragments[black]

To install the development and documentation dependencies:

pip install python-fragments[dev,docs]

docs.title: Register the loader
docs.text:
Add this import at your application's entry point, before any modules that contain fragments are imported:

from fragments import loader
from my_components import fragment_component

You may want to include an # isort: skip comment to make sure this import isn't automatically moved.

That's all. Any .py file containing <> will be transpiled automatically at import time.

docs.title: Language Server
docs.text: Type checking, completions, hover docs, go-to-definition, and rename work out of the box.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Diagnostics — type errors and undefined names reported inline
  • Hover — type information and docstrings on hover
  • Completions — attribute, method, and name completions including trigger-on-dot
  • Semantic tokens — type-aware syntax highlighting for Python code inside fragments
  • Syntax highlighting — structural highlighting for <>, tags, and {{ }} interpolations
  • Go-to-definition — jump to the definition of a symbol
  • Find references — list all usages of a symbol
  • Rename — rename a symbol across all files in the workspace
  • Formatting — formats the Python around fragments with the Black integration

All features work on component names and attribute names in component tags — go-to-definition on <Layout> jumps to the function, rename propagates across all usages, hover shows parameter types.

Not yet implemented:

  • Fragments-specific syntax — autocompletion and syntax highlighting for fragments blocks

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install python-fragments[lsp]

Then start the language server:

fragments-lsp

docs.title: VS Code
docs.text: Type checking, completions, hover docs, go-to-definition, and rename work out of the box.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install the Python Fragments extension from the VS Code Marketplace.

Install the Python extension and select the interpreter for the environment where python-fragments[lsp] is installed. The extension will automatically start fragments-lsp from that environment.

If a conflicting Python language server (such as Pylance) is active, the extension will prompt you to disable it on first activation.

docs.title: Building from source
docs.text:
Bump the package version if needed:

cd vscode-extension
npm version patch --no-git-tag-version # for a patch update
npm version minor --no-git-tag-version # for a minor update
npm version major --no-git-tag-version # for a major update
cd ..

To build and install the extension manually:

npm install -g @vscode/vsce
cd vscode-extension
npm install
vsce package
code --install-extension <filename>.vsix

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Setting Default Description fragments.serverPath (derived from active interpreter) Override path to the fragments-lsp executable. Only needed if auto-detection fails. fragments.blackArgs "" Extra Black options used when formatting, e.g. -l 100 --preview.

docs.title: Formatting
docs.text: Format on save is supported with the Black integration.

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text:
Most Python tooling can't parse fragment syntax: running a formatter or linter directly on a file containing <>...</> fails. Integrations connect Fragments to these tools, so they work on the Python in your fragment files without breaking the fragments.

Each integration is an optional extra. You only install the tools you use.

Category Tool Extra Command Formatting Black python-fragments[black] fragments black

Integrations are available in three places:

  • Command line — through the fragments command.
  • Editors — through the language server and the VS Code extension.
  • Pre-commit — through hooks published from this repository.

Each integration page says which of its tool's features are supported.

More integrations, including Ruff and import sorting, are on the roadmap.

docs.title: Black
docs.text: Format the Python in your fragment files with Black. Everything inside <>...</> is left exactly as written.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install python-fragments[black]

This installs a supported version of Black alongside Fragments.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Black can't parse fragment syntax, so Fragments does three things:

  1. Swaps each fragment for a placeholder name.
  2. Formats the resulting plain Python with Black.
  3. Puts the original fragments back.

Black's internal parser reads your configuration and command line options, so supported featuresbehave exactly as expected.

docs.title: Supported
docs.text:
• Formatting all the Python outside fragments, including expressions that contain inline fragments.
  • [tool.black] in pyproject.toml.
  • Black's command line options that control the code style, such as line length, string normalization, preview and target versions.
  • Black's file discovery: directories, .gitignore, include, exclude, extend-exclude and force-exclude.
  • --check, --diff and --quiet.
  • Format document and format on save in editors, through the language server.
  • A pre-commit hook.

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text:
• Formatting inside fragments. Tags, attributes and the Python inside {{ }} interpolations are not changed.
  • Notebooks and stubs. .ipynb and .pyi files are skipped when searching directories, and --ipynb and --pyi are rejected.
  • Partial formatting. --line-ranges is rejected, and editors can't format only a selection.
  • Standard input. --code, --stdin-filename and - are not supported.
  • Black's cache and parallel workers. --cache-dir, --no-cache and --workers are accepted but have no effect.
  • Files that don't parse. On the command line they're reported as path:line:column: message and the remaining files are still formatted. In editors they're left unchanged.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
fragments black src/ app.py      # format files or directories in place
fragments black --check src/     # exit 1 if any file would change
fragments black --diff app.py    # print a diff instead of writing
fragments black -l 100 -S src/   # any Black option, on top of [tool.black]
Exit code Meaning 0 Success 1 A file failed to parse, or --check found a file that would change 2 No files given, a path doesn't exist, an option is invalid or unsupported, or the configuration is invalid

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
fragments black accepts the following command line options:

Support Options Full -l, -t, -S, -C, --preview, --unstable, --enable-unstable-feature, --include, --exclude, --extend-exclude, --force-exclude, --config, --check, --diff, -q, -h, --version Ignore --fast/--safe, -W, --color/--no-color, -v, --required-version, --cache-dir, --no-cache None -c/--code, --pyi, --ipynb, --python-cell-magics, -x, --line-ranges, --stdin-filename

Ignored options are accepted but do nothing. Rejected options change what the input is, and ignoring them would silently give different output from what you asked for.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Settings are read from [tool.black] in the project's pyproject.toml See here for more. Command line options override them.

E.g:

[tool.black]
line-length = 100
skip-string-normalization = true

See Black's configuration docs for every setting.

docs.title: Excluding files
docs.text:
exclude and extend-exclude only apply when searching directories. A file named explicitly on the command line, or opened in an editor, is still formatted. To skip a file in every case, use force-exclude:

[tool.black]
force-exclude = '^/generated/'

docs.title: Editors
docs.text:
Install the lsp extra as well:

pip install python-fragments[lsp,black]

The language server then provides document formatting. Black's options can be passed in the fragments.blackArgs setting, a string such as "-l 100 --preview". The server requests it from the editor with workspace/configuration each time it formats a document, so changes apply immediately.

The setting accepts the same options as fragments black, with these differences:

  • File paths, -h and --version are rejected.
  • --check, --diff and -q have no effect.

Black caches the pyproject.toml it reads, so restart the language server after changing [tool.black].

docs.title: VS Code
docs.text:
Make Python Fragments the formatter for Python files:

{
  "[python]": {
    "editor.defaultFormatter": "tra-technologies-ltd.python-fragments",
    "editor.formatOnSave": true
  },
  "fragments.blackArgs": "-l 100 --preview"
}

After changing [tool.black], run Python Fragments: Restart Server.

docs.title: Pre-commit
docs.text:
Run Black on every commit with pre-commit.

  1. Install pre-commit:

    pip install pre-commit

  2. Add the hook to .pre-commit-config.yaml in the root of your repository:

    repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/TheRunningAlgorithm2/python-fragments
    rev: v0.37
    hooks:
      - id: fragments-black

    Or use a local hook that runs the fragments already installed in your environment:

    repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: fragments-black
        name: fragments black
        entry: fragments black
        language: system
        types: [python]

  3. Install the git hook:

    pre-commit install

  4. Optionally, format everything already in the repository:

    pre-commit run fragments-black --all-files

The hook formats staged files in place. If it changes anything, the commit is stopped so you can review the changes and git add them. Files without fragments are formatted as normal Python, so the hook is safe to run on every .py file.

Pass Black options with the hook's args: key:

        hooks:
          - id: fragments-black
            args: [--line-length, "100", --preview]

Use instead of a Black hook

Black itself can't parse fragment syntax. Don't run a separate Black hook on the same files: fragments-black replaces it.

Pre-commit passes each staged file by name, so only force-exclude applies (see Excluding files). You can also use pre-commit's own exclude: key on the hook.

docs.title: Running in CI
docs.text:
Use --check to fail without changing any files:

fragments black --check .

docs.title: String attributes (default)
docs.text:
Plain string values work exactly as in HTML:

<button type="submit">Save</button>

docs.title: Expression attributes
docs.text:
Use {{ }} to pass any Python expression as an attribute value:

<a href={{ page.url }} id={{ page.slug }}>{{ page.title }}</a>

docs.title: Boolean attributes
docs.text:
Attributes with no value are passed through as-is:

<input type="checkbox" checked />

When using an interpolated value, fragments does not treat Python booleans specially — True and False are rendered as the strings "true" and "false" respectively:

<input type="checkbox" checked={{ is_checked }} />
# is_checked=True  → <input type="checkbox" checked="true" />
# is_checked=False → <input type="checkbox" checked="false" />

To omit an attribute entirely, pass None:

<input type="checkbox" checked={{ is_checked or None }} />
# is_checked=True  → <input type="checkbox" checked="true" />
# is_checked=False → <input type="checkbox" />

docs.title: Style
docs.text:
The style attribute accepts a dict. Keys are CSS property names, values are strings:

styles = {"color": "red", "font-weight": "bold"}

return <>
    <p style={{ styles }}>Important</p>
</>

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
As class is a reserved keyword in Python, use classes instead. It accepts a plain string or a list of strings:

<div classes="card"></div>
<div classes={{ "card" }}></div>
<div classes={{ ["card", "highlighted"] }}></div>
<div classes={{ active_classes }}></div>

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
HTML comments use the standard <!-- --> syntax and can appear anywhere inside a fragment:

def my_view() -> str:
    return <>
        <!-- page header -->
        <h1>Hello</h1>
        <p>Welcome.</p>
    </>

Comments are passed through to the rendered HTML output unchanged:

<!-- page header --><h1>Hello</h1><p>Welcome.</p>

docs.title: Inside elements
docs.text:
Comments can appear as children of any HTML element:

<ul>
    <!-- items are filtered before rendering -->
    <li for={{ item in published_items }}>{{ item.name }}</li>
</ul>

docs.title: Multiline comments
docs.text:
Comments may span multiple lines:

<>
    <!--
        TODO: replace with a dynamic component once the API is ready
    -->
    <div classes="placeholder">Coming soon</div>
</>

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Any Python function can be used as a component. Components are distinguished from HTML elements by their name: an uppercase first letter means a component call, lowercase means a standard HTML element.

Template is a reserved name

<Template> is a built-in element for control flow, so a function named Template cannot be used as a component. Names that only start with Template, such as TemplateCard, are unaffected.

docs.title: Defining a component
docs.text:
A component is a plain Python function that returns a fragment. Attributes passed on the tag become keyword arguments — declare them explicitly or accept them all with **kwargs:

from fragments.types import Children

def Card(children: Children, classes: str = "") -> str:
    return <>
        <div classes={{ classes }}>
            <Children... />
        </div>
    </>

Use <Children... /> inside the component body to mark where the caller's children should be rendered. It is always self-closing and takes no attributes.

docs.title: Using a component
docs.text:
Use it like an HTML tag:

return <>
    <Card>
        <p>Some content</p>
    </Card>
</>

Attributes on the tag are forwarded as keyword arguments to the function:

<Card classes="featured">
    <p>Highlighted content</p>
</Card>

docs.title: Self-closing components
docs.text:
Components with no children can use self-closing syntax:

<Avatar src={{ user.avatar_url }} />

Self-closing components receive no children argument, so there is no need to declare a children parameter:

def Avatar(src: str) -> str:
    return <>
        <img src={{ src }} alt="avatar" />
    </>

docs.title: Conditional rendering
docs.text:
Add an if attribute to any element to render it conditionally:

return <>
    <p if={{ user.is_admin }}>Admin panel</p>
    <p if={{ not user.is_verified }}>Please verify your email.</p>
</>

The element is omitted entirely from the output when the condition is false.

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
Add a for attribute to repeat an element over any iterable:

return <>
    <ul>
        <li for={{ item in cart.items }}>
            {{ item.name }} — {{ item.price }}
        </li>
    </ul>
</>

if and for can be combined on the same element:

<li for={{ post in posts }} if={{ post.published }}>
    {{ post.title }}
</li>

When combined, if filters each item, reading like for post in posts if post.published. It is evaluated once per item and can refer to the loop variable. The order of the two attributes does not matter.

docs.title: Template
docs.text:
Use <Template> to apply if or for to a group of elements without wrapping them in an extra element. <Template> renders only its children:

return <>
    <dl>
        <Template for={{ term in glossary }}>
            <dt>{{ term.name }}</dt>
            <dd>{{ term.definition }}</dd>
        </Template>
    </dl>
</>

if and for work on <Template> exactly as they do on elements, including when combined:

<Template for={{ post in posts }} if={{ post.published }}>
    <h2>{{ post.title }}</h2>
    <p>{{ post.summary }}</p>
</Template>

To check a condition once for a whole loop, rather than once per item, nest two templates:

<Template if={{ user.is_admin }}>
    <Template for={{ report in reports }}>
        <ReportRow report={{ report }} />
    </Template>
</Template>

<Template> only accepts if and for attributes, and both must be interpolations. It cannot be self-closing. A <Template> with no attributes is allowed and simply renders its children.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
if and for work on component tags too:

<PostCard for={{ post in published }} post={{ post }} />
<Banner if={{ show_banner }} />

They are purely structural — the transpiler handles them before the call is emitted, so neither if nor for is ever passed as a keyword argument to the component function.

docs.title: Fragments
docs.text:
A fragment is a block of HTML written inline in Python, delimited by <> and </>. At runtime, a fragment is transpiled into a function call that returns a plain Python string - so you can use one anywhere you would use a string.

def my_view():
    return <>
        <h1>Hello</h1>
        <p>Welcome.</p>
    </>

Fragments must be wrapped in <> and </>, return <MyComponent /> is not valid syntax

Because a fragment evaluates to a string, it can appear as a return value, in an assignment, passed as an argument, or in any other string context:

<> and </> inside Python string literals or line comments are not treated as fragment delimiters, so code like assert result == "<p>hello</p>" or # renders a <> fragment </> is safe.

# As a return value
def my_view() -> str:
    return <>
        <h1>Hello</h1>
    </>

# In an assignment
html = <><p>Some content</p></>

# Passed as an argument
response = HTMLResponse(<><h1>Hello</h1></>)

docs.title: Interpolation
docs.text:
Embed any Python expression inside {{ }}:

def greeting(name: str):
    return <>
        <h1>Hello, {{ name }}!</h1>
        <p>You have {{ len(messages) }} messages.</p>
    </>

The same syntax works in attribute values — see Attributes for details.

docs.title: Scripts and styles
docs.text:
Interpolation is not supported inside <script> or <style> bodies, where {{ }} is plain text (see Scripts and Styles). To pass data to a script, use an attribute instead. Dicts and lists are JSON-encoded and HTML-escaped:

<div id="app" data-config={{ config }}></div>
<script>
    const config = JSON.parse(document.getElementById("app").dataset.config);
</script>

docs.title: Scripts and Styles
docs.text:
The bodies of <script> and <style> elements are raw text. They are passed through to the rendered HTML exactly as written, including all whitespace and indentation:

def page() -> str:
    return <>
        <style>
            .card > h2 { margin: 0; }
        </style>
        <script>
            if (count < limit) {
                console.log("under the limit");
            }
        </script>
    </>

No fragment syntax is recognised inside the body. <, {{ }}, <!-- --> and </> are all plain text there, so JavaScript and CSS can be written without any escaping.

docs.title: Closing tags
docs.text:
The body ends at the first matching closing tag. It is matched case-sensitively, and whitespace is allowed before the >:

<script>console.log("hello")</script >

</SCRIPT> and </script/> do not end the body. As in a browser, a </script> inside a JavaScript string does end it, so write <\/script> instead.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
Attributes work exactly as they do on any other element, including expression attributes and control flow:

<script src={{ static_url("app.js") }} nonce={{ csp_nonce }} defer></script>
<style if={{ dark_mode }}>
    body { background: black; }
</style>

docs.title: Self-closing tags
docs.text:
A self-closing <script /> is transpiled as written. Browsers do not treat <script /> as closed: they treat it as an opening tag, and everything after it becomes part of the script. Always write an explicit closing tag:

<script src="app.js"></script>

docs.title: HTML Library
docs.text:
The transpiler generates f-strings directly for HTML elements, and imports two runtime helpers from fragments.html.elements for the cases that need them.

attribute_to_string(name, value) renders a single HTML attribute. It is called inside f-string interpolations in the transpiled code whenever an attribute has a dynamic value.

Argument Type Purpose name str The attribute name value Any The attribute value

All values are HTML-escaped before being inserted into the attribute string, so characters like ", &, <, and > in dynamic values are always safe.

Special cases handled automatically:

  • className — converted to class="...". Accepts a string or a list of strings (joined with spaces).
  • style — converted to style="...". Accepts a string or a dict of CSS properties.
  • None — omits the attribute entirely.
  • dict or list — JSON-encoded.

comment(content) renders an HTML comment — it is what <!-- ... --> compiles to.

docs.title: Import Hook
docs.text:
When you import fragments.loader, it installs a custom MetaPathFinder on sys.meta_path. From that point on, every .py file that Python imports is intercepted. If the file contains <>, the source is transpiled before it reaches the interpreter. Files without <> pass through unchanged.

from fragments import loader  # installs the hook — must come first

from fastapi import FastAPI   # any fragment-containing module imported after
from routes import router     # this line is now transpiled automatically

The hook operates on source text, so nothing is written to disk — your .py files are never modified.

docs.title: Transpilation
docs.text: Python does not natively understand <> or HTML tags inside .py files. Fragments solves this with a source-level transpiler that converts fragment syntax into plain Python at import time — so there is no build step.

docs.title: A simple example
docs.text:
Source code

from fragments import loader  # isort: skip

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/", response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def index() -> str:
    return <>
        <h1>Hello, world!</h1>
        <p>Welcome to Fragments.</p>
    </>

After transpilation — what the interpreter sees:

from fragments.html.elements import attribute_to_string, comment
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/", response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def index() -> str:
    return ""+f"<h1>"+"Hello, world!"+"</h1>"+f"<p>"+"Welcome to Fragments."+"</p>"

Endpoint return value — a plain Python string:

'<h1>Hello, world!</h1><p>Welcome to Fragments.</p>'

The transpiler does two things:

  1. Prepends from fragments.html.elements import attribute_to_string, comment at the top of the file.
  2. Replaces every <> ... </> block with an empty string "" followed by its children joined by +. Interpolated values are wrapped in str(...) so any type can be concatenated.

docs.title: Dynamic content — for and if
docs.text:
The for attribute on an element compiles to a generator expression wrapped in ''.join(str(...) for ...) so the result is a flat string.

Before:

@app.get("/posts", response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def post_list() -> str:
    posts = get_posts()
    return <>
        <h1>Posts</h1>
        <article for={{ post in posts }}>
            <h2>{{ post.title }}</h2>
            <p>{{ post.summary }}</p>
        </article>
    </>

After:

@app.get("/posts", response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def post_list() -> str:
    posts = get_posts()
    return ""+f"<h1>"+"Posts"+"</h1>"+''.join(str(f"<article>"+f"<h2>"+str(post.title)+"</h2>"+f"<p>"+str(post.summary)+"</p>"+"</article>") for post in posts)

Result (with two posts in the list):

'<h1>Posts</h1><article><h2>First Post</h2><p>A short summary.</p></article><article><h2>Second Post</h2><p>Another summary.</p></article>'

The for={{ post in posts }} attribute is stripped from the element and becomes the for post in posts clause of a generator expression. ''.join(str(...) for post in posts) then joins the resulting rendered articles into a flat string.

Similarly, if={{ condition }} on its own compiles to a Python ternary: (element if (condition) else '').

When for and if appear on the same element, the if becomes the filter clause of the generator expression, so it is evaluated once per item and can refer to the loop variable:

# <article for={{ post in posts }} if={{ post.published }}>...</article>
''.join(str(f"<article>"+...+"</article>") for post in posts if (post.published))

The condition is always wrapped in parentheses, so conditions such as a if b else c are valid in both forms.

docs.title: <Template>
docs.text:
<Template> produces no tags of its own. It compiles to its children joined onto an empty string, the same as a fragment, and its for and if attributes are applied to that string:

# <Template for={{ post in posts }}><h2>{{ post.title }}</h2><p>{{ post.summary }}</p></Template>
''.join(str(""+f"<h2>"+str(post.title)+"</h2>"+f"<p>"+str(post.summary)+"</p>") for post in posts)

docs.title: Components — uppercase tags
docs.text:
A tag whose name starts with an uppercase letter is treated as a component call rather than an HTML element. The tag name is used directly as a function reference, and the element's children and attributes are passed as arguments.

Before:

return <>
    <Layout title="My Blog">
        <h1>Posts</h1>
        <PostCard for={{ post in posts }} post={{ post }} />
    </Layout>
</>

After:

return ""+Layout(children=""+f"<h1>"+"Posts"+"</h1>"+''.join(str(PostCard(post=post,)) for post in posts),title="My Blog",)

Layout and PostCard are ordinary Python functions. The transpiler passes children as a keyword argument named children (a pre-joined string) and tag attributes as additional keyword arguments. Self-closing components receive no children argument at all. How kwargs are received is up to the component:

from fragments.types import Children

# Components that receive children declare a children parameter
def Layout(children: Children, **kwargs: Any) -> str: ...
def Card(children: Children, classes: str = "") -> str: ...

# Self-closing components need no children parameter
def PostCard(post: Post) -> str: ...

Explicit parameters give you full type checking, refactoring support, and IDE completions with no extra tooling.
